If you're not monitoring your SQS queue depth, you're basically flying blind. Your app could be drowning and you wouldn't even know it.


Queue depth is how many messages are sitting in your SQS queue waiting to be processed. If it keeps climbing, that's your signal that consumers are slower than producers — meaning jobs are piling up and users are getting delayed responses. Set a CloudWatch alarm on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and actually look at it. Catch the backlog before it becomes a disaster.

#AWS #SQS #Monitoring #CloudWatch #DevOps

concept: AWS SQS pricing and when to use it
tweet:
AWS SQS is basically a mailbox for your serverless apps. Messages wait in line until something picks them up. Problem: you're paying for every message, even the ones sitting there doing nothing.


SQS charges you per million requests, not per message stored. So if you queue up 10k messages but only process 100 today, you still pay for all 10k requests that created them.

This is why people use SQS for async tasks (send emails, process images) but switch to SNS or Kinesis for high-volume stuff. Also pro tip: use SQS FIFO if order matters, but it costs more and is slower.

Gotcha nobody talks about: batch your message sends. Instead of 1000 single requests, send 10 batches of 100. Same work, way cheaper.

#AWS #Serverless #SQS #CostOptimization #DevOps

Your ALB is probably doing work it shouldn't. Most teams don't use sticky sessions right.


Sticky sessions make sure the same user always hits the same server. Sounds good, right? But here's the thing: if that server dies, your user loses their session anyway.

Better move? Store sessions in a database or cache like Redis. Then ANY server can handle your user. That's actual reliability.

ALB sticky sessions are only useful if you're running old code that needs them. New apps? Skip it. Your load balancer shouldn't be a memory bank.

#DevOps #AWS #LoadBalancer #WebServers

Your EC2 instance has a git repo but you never commit. Then it crashes. Everything you coded? Gone forever.


This is why you push to GitHub. Your code should live somewhere safe, not just on one machine.

Think of git commits like saving your game. If you don't save, you lose progress. If you only save on your laptop, and your laptop breaks, that game is gone.

With EC2, same deal. Your code needs to be in a git repo (GitHub, GitLab, whatever). Then if the instance dies, you spin up a new one, clone the repo, and you're back in business.

Pro tip: Use git hooks to auto-deploy when you push. Your EC2 pulls the latest code automatically. One command, everything updates.

#Git #EC2 #DevOps #CloudComputing

hook: Most engineers using Aurora don't know this: your read replicas won't auto-scale with your writes. Here's why 👇
thread:
Aurora is smart about spreading reads across replicas. But those replicas don't grow in size when your main DB gets hammered.

Think of it like a restaurant. The main kitchen (writer) can expand. But if you add more waiters (read replicas), they're still serving food from the same kitchen.

The gotcha: Aurora scales OUT (more replicas) but not UP (bigger replicas). Your write capacity is still capped by that one main DB.

So if your writes are the problem, adding read replicas won't help. You need to scale the main instance itself.

Pro tip: Monitor your writer CPU and connections. That's your real bottleneck, not replica count.

What's your biggest Aurora scaling headache? Reads or writes? 👇

#Aurora #AWS #Database

concept: SNS as broadcast vs queue storage
hook: Most engineers use SNS wrong and don't realize it. Here's what nobody tells you 👇
thread:
SNS is NOT a queue. It's a megaphone.

You publish a message once. SNS shouts it to everyone listening at the same time. Then it's gone.

Compare that to SQS (a real queue). Messages sit there waiting. Workers grab one. Process it. Delete it.

SNS = broadcast
SQS = line at the store

Gotcha: If nobody's listening when SNS broadcasts, the message vanishes. No replay. This trips people up hard.

Use SNS when you want multiple systems to react to something NOW. Use SQS when work needs to wait in line.

So here's the real question: Are you using SNS for things that actually need a queue? What would you change? 👇

#DevOps #AWS #SNS #DatabaseFundamentals
